criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1: Although household use is mentioned in passing among competing freshwater uses, the article examines rural freshwater resource politics across three resource/production sectors—agricultural irrigation and drainage, hydropower and large dams, and industrial water pollution—rather than household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: This paper passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2 because it discusses legal, institutional, and governance arrangements for water resources in China (such as the 1988 and 2002 Water Laws, state vs. collective ownership, Self-Funded Irrigation and Drainage Districts, water abstraction charges/permits, tiao/kuai bureaucratic authority, and pollution litigation). However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading because these institutions are examined as macro-level water-resource allocation, agricultural irrigation water rights, hydropower project governance, and industrial pollution torts rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. (Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude due to lack of empirical evidence/systematic synthesis and lack of household/community service-access outcomes.)
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05): The article is a narrative, non-systematic review essay surveying selected English-language scholarship on rural water politics in China. It contains no primary empirical data collection or analysis and has no systematic review methodology (no search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, study selection, or structured synthesis).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: Reports no primary or systematically synthesized outcomes measuring household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion; discussion centers on secondary accounts of grain yields, aquifer depletion, dam resettlement, and river pollution.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5: As a narrative overview essay without primary data or systematic review methods, there is no identifiable empirical study population/sample, exposure, access outcome, or empirical study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies Criterion 6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This contribution reviews a small but important body of scholarship on rural water politics in China, identifying existing themes and suggesting new directions where scholarship is currently lacking.
The most developed and important body of work revolves around irrigation water management.

According to the Water Law of the People’s Republic of China, all water is the property of the central state or of the collective; thus, the simple answer to the above questions is that water is a public good not tradable for private gain, and not available to be owned by any entity other than the state or its rural extensions
Whereas prior to 1988 water had been essentially treated as an open-access resource, the 1988 Water Law sought to institutionalize on a national level its management
In this paper I have reviewed scholarship on the institutions, discourses and power relations that shape water politics in rural China and thereby constrain or facilitate access to water.

raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Magee (2013) is a narrative literature review essay of English-language scholarship on rural water politics in China with no primary empirical data and no systematic empirical synthesis methodology. Furthermore, the review focuses on macro/sectoral freshwater resource competition across agricultural irrigation and drainage, hydropower dams, and industrial river pollution rather than rule-type legal/administrative mechanisms governing household or community water or sanitation service access.
